title: How AI apocalypse fears are reshaping the stock market's AI trade
excerpt: A potential AI slowdown is separating the stock market's new winners and losers.
content_html:
The AI trade is already sketching its playbook for a possible apocalypse

By Joe Ciolli

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Author of the First Trade newsletter

Up until this point, the AI trade has taken countless licks and kept on ticking.

There's been near-incessant bubble talk, questions over AI's returns, backlash against debt-funded spending, energy constraints, and a painful memory-stock unwind. Yet the trade has put its head down and moved past each.

It now faces its most abstract pair of risks yet: the prospect that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity, and a possible slowdown championed by some of the industry's biggest names.

The developments have been enough to give investors whiplash, especially considering that — until this latest bout of AI skepticism — stocks were hovering within shouting distance of record highs.

Monday's market action offered an early investing playbook for a world where AI development slows. At the index level, the reaction was barely a blip. The S&P 500 fell just 0.5%, masking a much sharper rotation beneath the surface.

After all, a recalibrated pace won't kill the AI trade entirely. It will instead create a new dynamic, forcing investors to rethink which sectors benefit from — or get hurt by — greater safety efforts.

Here's what the market is saying investors should buy, sell, and watch:

1. Buy cybersecurity

The move on Monday: CrowdStrike jumped 14%, Palo Alto Networks gained 13%, and the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF rose 6%, even as the broader market fell.

The significance: If AI makes cyberattacks faster, cheaper, and more sophisticated, spending on security will become non-negotiable. This gives cybersecurity a useful hedge-like quality. Regardless of whether the AI race accelerates or slows, companies and governments will need stronger defenses.

2. Buy companies threatened by AI disruption

The move on Monday: IGV, the market's biggest software ETF, rose 5% on Monday, while Adobe, ServiceNow, and Workday gained between 5% and 7%.

The significance: Software companies have spent much of the year in a particularly awkward spot: They must invest heavily in AI while worrying that it could upend their own businesses. A slower, more safety-conscious rollout could ease both pressures. This dynamic extends to any AI-exposed subsector, with software as the best example.

3. Buy established platforms

The move on Monday: A-list hyperscalers Alphabet and Meta each rose about 3%, breaking from the broader AI-linked sell-off.

The significance: A more safety-conscious AI era may favor companies with ample cash, global distribution, and already-entrenched businesses. Alphabet and Meta can afford a slower route to monetization in a way smaller, less diversified AI bets cannot.

4. Sell or trim the pure AI-buildout trade

The move on Monday: The Roundhill Memory ETF fell 7%, while the broader Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost 6%. Major industry players like Nvidia, Micron, SanDisk, and SK Hynix were among those to drop.

The significance: Companies that sell the physical backbone of the AI boom need the infrastructure buildout to keep accelerating to justify their valuations. They're already the most crowded part of the trade, so any pause from safety concerns, regulation, or slower spending could hurt them disproportionately.

It's amazing what the market can show us in just one day after a sudden shock to the system. We now have an early framework for how investors could respond in a more security-conscious AI era. It's ultimately a good reminder that the AI trade doesn't go away when the story changes — it just changes its stripes.
